sources_considered.why: The cited story, bylined Connie Loizos, published 2026-02-09.
METR's note that AI agents code much faster than humans, used as context for 'wicked fast'.
Secondary and not about coders specifically. The TechCrunch piece was enough.

receipt.public_excerpt: As one engineer told them, “You had thought that maybe, oh, because you could be more productive with AI, then you save some time, you can work less. But then really, you don’t work less. You just work the same amount or even more.”

evidence_items.explanation: The Loizos story exists and reports an engineer at an AI-embracing tech company describing more work, not less.

receipt.public_excerpt: expectations have tripled, stress has tripled and actual productivity has only gone up by maybe 10%.

evidence_items.explanation: The story quotes a tech worker reporting stress that has tripled against a gain of about 10%. That matches 'modest gains relative to that burnout'.

receipt.public_excerpt: It confirms it, then shows where all that augmentation actually leads, which is “fatigue, burnout, and a growing sense that work is harder to step away from, especially as organizational expectations for speed and responsiveness rise,” according to the researchers.

evidence_items.explanation: The underlying UC Berkeley/HBR research reports burnout among AI adopters. It also says the augmentation is real, which tempers the 'modest gains' part.

evidence_items.locator: FAQ 'How long do AI agents take to complete a 2-hour task?'

receipt.public_excerpt: This is also partly because many AI agents code much faster than human software engineers.

evidence_items.explanation: This backs the uncontroversial 'wicked fast' framing. The page version read is dated after the post, so it is context only.

unresolved_gaps: The Berkeley study covers workers at one 200-person tech company, not only coders, and its gains were not quantified in the story.
The 10% figure is one anonymous forum commenter.
